title: Error Handling: TRY/CATCH, RAISERROR, and THROW
description: Gracefully handle exceptions with TRY/CATCH, diagnose errors using ERROR_* functions, and raise custom errors with RAISERROR and THROW.

data.text: No production database is immune to errors: a bad division, a missing table, a constraint violation. The difference between a robust system and a fragile one is how you handle those errors. SQL Server gives you TRY/CATCH for catching exceptions, and RAISERROR and THROW for raising your own.
TRY...CATCH is SQL Server's exception handler. Statements that might fail go in the BEGIN TRY block. If any throws an error, control jumps to the BEGIN CATCH block — skipping everything in between.

data.title: TRY...CATCH structure
Scope of TRY/CATCH
data.text: TRY/CATCH must be in the same batch — you cannot open a TRY in one stored procedure and close the CATCH in another. However, if a called procedure errors, the CATCH in the calling batch still fires.
Inside a CATCH block, six functions give you full details about what went wrong. They all return NULL outside a CATCH block:

rows: The state (1-255) — helps distinguish identical errors
Name of the procedure or trigger where the error occurred
Line number within the procedure where the error occurred

data.title: Logging error details
data.code:
BEGIN TRY
    INSERT INTO sales.orders (customer_id, order_date)
    VALUES (99999, GETDATE());
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    SELECT
        ERROR_NUMBER()    AS ErrorNumber,
        ERROR_MESSAGE()   AS ErrorMessage,
        ERROR_PROCEDURE() AS ErrorProcedure,
        ERROR_LINE()      AS ErrorLine
        ERROR_SEVERITY()  AS ErrorSeverity,
        ERROR_STATE()   AS ErrorState;
END CATCH;

data.title: Log to a table
data.text: In production, insert error details into a dedicated log table (with columns for timestamp, procedure, error number, message, and user) so errors are auditable even if nobody is watching SSMS.
When TRY/CATCH wraps a transaction, you need to decide whether to COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The XACT_STATE() function tells you the transaction's health:

rows: Uncommittable — the transaction has errored and cannot commit
Committable — the transaction is still healthy

data.title: Safe transfer with transaction rollback

data.text: RAISERROR — the legacy way to raise errors
RAISERROR (Transact-SQL) lets you raise a custom error with a message, severity, and state. It can also re-throw an existing error from a CATCH block by using ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_MESSAGE(), etc.

data.title: RAISERROR with severity and state

data.text: THROW was introduced in SQL Server 2012 as a simpler replacement for RAISERROR. It requires less syntax and always produces a standard error — but it cannot format messages or set a custom severity.

rows: Just write THROW with no args

data.title: Re-throwing the original error
THROW vs RAISERROR in new code
data.text: For new code on SQL Server 2012+, prefer THROW for simple re-throws and RAISERROR when you need custom severity or formatted messages (e.g., with %s placeholders).

data.title: Error handling essentials
points: TRY/CATCH catches exceptions — all failing statements jump to the CATCH block
ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_LINE() etc. give full error details in CATCH
XACT_STATE() tells you if a transaction is committable (-1 = no, 1 = yes, 0 = none)
RAISERROR offers severity/state control and message formatting
THROW is simpler for re-throwing and works with no arguments, but can't set severity
